items.question: Why do you focus on token efficiency rather than simply making model training faster?
items.object: Token efficiency versus training or compute efficiency
items.answer: We wanted to maximize the use of every piece of data—what is called token efficiency. You want the brain to grow more from eating the same amount of data; you want to get more intelligence. This differs somewhat from earlier lines of thinking. It is interesting because it produces a relatively large improvement in token efficiency. items.question: How do you see the connection between managing a team and creating new scientific knowledge?
items.object: Team management and scientific research as reinforcement-learning processes
items.answer: Recently I have been thinking about something: several things seem somewhat connected. If you look at the process of doing scientific research or creating new knowledge, it resembles a reinforcement-learning process. One theory, empiricism, says people gain new knowledge from experience. Later, of course, many views argued otherwise. Humans have existed on Earth for a very, very long time, yet perhaps three or four hundred years ago no one said the Earth was a sphere. We were always in that experience, but did not know what the facts were. So experience cannot directly give you knowledge. Rather, you propose a hypothesis: you observe some things, then hypothesize that perhaps the Earth is round, and try every possible way to verify it. Likewise, in training neural networks, you may observe hundreds of thousands of kernel metrics and find that some seem wrong. Direct observation does not give you new knowledge; you propose a hypothesis as to why it is that way, then design experiments to verify it. This is probably what we now consider a good method—indeed, perhaps all good scientific research works this way. These things seem interconnected. You find that managing a team also works this way: you need to manage with RL.
